title: The Supreme Court Just Cleared Reliance of Fraud in a ₹447 Crore Market Manipulation Case.
excerpt: India's apex court overturned SEBI's finding that Mukesh Ambani's company rigged Reliance Petroleum futures in 2007. It ordered SEBI to refund ₹250 crore. The ₹25 crore regulatory penalty stays.
body:
Nearly two decades of litigation over one of India's most complex securities fraud cases ended on Friday when the Supreme Court set aside the Securities and Exchange Board of India's order directing Reliance Industries to return ₹447.27 crore in alleged illegal profits.

The case dates to November 2007, when Reliance Industries decided to sell roughly 5 percent of its stake in its then-subsidiary, Reliance Petroleum Ltd. SEBI alleged that before the sale, RIL entered into arrangements with 12 entities that built substantial short positions in RPL futures contracts. On the day the futures expired — November 29, 2007 — Reliance sold about 1.95 crore RPL shares in the cash market during the final minutes of trading, depressing the price. The short positions profited. SEBI estimated the gain at approximately ₹513 crore.

In March 2017, SEBI ruled that the scheme amounted to fraud and market manipulation. It ordered RIL to disgorge ₹447.27 crore plus 12 percent annual interest from 2007. The Securities Appellate Tribunal upheld that order in November 2020 by majority decision.

On Friday, a Supreme Court bench overturned both.

## Hedging Is Not Fraud

The core of the Supreme Court's reasoning was a distinction between regulatory violations and criminal fraud. The court found that while RIL and its associated entities had breached position limits in the derivatives market — a regulatory infraction — that breach did not, by itself, constitute market manipulation.

**"There is no legal requirement to ensure a perfect hedge with a 1:1 ratio,"** the court said. It held that hedging is a legitimate risk-management tool, and SEBI had failed to meet the higher burden of proof required to establish that Reliance's trading constituted a deliberate scheme to manipulate settlement prices.

The court distinguished between the adjudicating officer's penalty proceedings and the whole-time member's disgorgement order. It upheld the ₹25 crore penalty that SEBI's adjudicating officer had imposed on RIL for regulatory breaches, including failure to meet disclosure obligations. But it vacated the far larger ₹447.27 crore disgorgement, ruling that the fraud finding underpinning it was not supported by sufficient evidence.

## ₹250 Crore Ordered Refunded

When the Supreme Court admitted RIL's appeal in 2021, it had ordered the company to deposit ₹250 crore in SEBI's Investors' Protection Fund as an interim measure. On Friday, the court directed SEBI to refund that amount.

RIL was represented by Senior Advocates Harish Salve and Ritin Rai. SEBI was represented by Senior Advocates Arvind Datar and Pratap Venugopal.

## What SEBI Alleged

The regulator's case rested on the coordination between RIL and 12 entities: Chintamani Holdings, Devarshi Commercial, Darshan Mercantile, Dhriti Investments, Fiascon Holdings, Gandhar Trading, Harish Textiles Engineers, Mahalaxmi Glass Works, Mesmore Investment, Priority Constructions, Siddhivinayak Investment, and Titanium Investments. SEBI said these entities built futures positions equivalent to nearly 9.92 crore shares — well beyond regulatory limits — and that the profits flowed back to RIL.

The regulator also pointed to the timing of the cash market sale: 1.95 crore shares dumped in the final 10 minutes of trading on expiry day, a pattern it said was designed to depress the settlement price.

The Supreme Court acknowledged the circumstantial evidence but held that SEBI had not demonstrated that the trading pattern rose to the level of fraud under the Prevention of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices Regulations.

## Ambani Cleared Earlier

This is the second Supreme Court victory for Reliance in proceedings stemming from the same 2007 RPL episode. In November 2024, the court had quashed SEBI's ₹15 crore penalty against RIL chairman Mukesh Ambani personally, after the SAT found that SEBI had failed to establish Ambani's direct involvement in the trades. Board minutes showed the transactions were executed by two senior officials without his knowledge.

## What It Means for Markets

The ruling narrows the scope of what regulators can characterize as market manipulation in India's derivatives markets. By holding that exceeding position limits is a regulatory violation but not necessarily fraud, the court has drawn a clearer line between enforcement actions that carry penalties and those that can trigger disgorgement — a distinction that will shape future SEBI enforcement actions.

For NRI investors with exposure to Reliance — one of the most widely held Indian stocks globally — the ruling removes a long-standing legal overhang. RIL's market capitalization exceeds $230 billion, and the company is a core holding in virtually every India-focused mutual fund and ETF.
